title: 道德經 第六十五章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 65, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 85. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 65 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 淳德 (Plain Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
古之善為道者，
非以明民，
將以愚之。

morph.gloss: to be good at, to do well at
to do, to practise (wéi — the house default; nothing benefactive here)
the ones who — it closes the whole phrase and makes it a noun
not — it negates the whole purpose that follows
bright, clear-sighted — here an adjective used as a causative verb: to make bright
the people, the common folk — the ruled, as against their ruler
will, is going to — the plain adverb of intent, standing before its verb (the same 將 as 天將救之 in chapter 67); answering the 非 of the line before, it comes out as 'but will rather'
simple, unknowing — again an adjective as causative verb: to make simple

sentences.l:
Of old, the ones good at doing the Way —
not by it to make the people bright,
but by it to make them simple.
sentences.i: Those of old who were good at the Way did not use it to make the people knowing, but to keep them simple.
sentences.n:
古之善為道者 is this book's standing way of pointing backwards: 'of old, the ones good at ——'. 者 does the holding-together; it turns everything in front of it into a noun.

明 is 'clear-sighted, discerning', not the 智 'cleverness' of the next unit — the chapter keeps them apart and so does the English. 明 and 愚 are both adjectives doing duty as causative verbs. 明民 is not 'the bright people' but 'to make the people bright', and 愚之 'to make them simple'. Nothing marks the shift — no ending, no particle; only the slot the character stands in. 之 is the object pronoun here, 'them'.

This is the chapter that gets held against the book, and there is no softening it: it says the ruler should keep the people unknowing. Wang Bi at least says what he takes 愚 to mean — 無知守真順自然, 'without cleverness, keeping to what is genuine, going along with what is so of itself' — and 愚 was already a compliment in chapter 20, where the speaker calls his own mind 愚人之心, a fool's heart. Whether that is what the line meant, or a later reader making it bearable, is left to you.

sentences.t:
民之難治，
以其智多。

morph.gloss: the people, the common folk — the ruled, as against their ruler
(particle) — dropped between a subject and its predicate, it makes the whole clause a noun
hard to, difficult to (nán; read nàn it is the noun 'a calamity')
to govern, to bring into order
because of — 以 in its causal sense, not the instrumental one
cleverness, shrewd calculation — not wisdom in the good sense

sentences.l:
The people's being hard to govern —
because their cleverness is much.
sentences.i: The people are hard to govern because they know too much.
sentences.n:
A third job for 之, and the last one you need. Dropped between a subject and what is said of it, it dissolves the sentence into a noun phrase: 民難治 would be 'the people are hard to govern', but 民之難治 is 'the people's being hard to govern'. You have already met 之 as 'of' and as 'them'; one character, three jobs, and only position to tell them apart.

以 has swung too. In the unit above it was instrumental, 'by means of'; here it is causal, 'because of'. Same character, and only the sense of the line decides.

智 is not wisdom. It is cleverness — the shrewdness that calculates and contrives, which this book distrusts wherever it finds it.

sentences.t:
故以智治國，
國之賊，

morph.gloss: a robber who takes by force; as a verb, to do violence to

sentences.l:
Therefore: to govern the state by cleverness —
the state's robber;
sentences.i: So: to govern a state by cleverness is to rob it;
sentences.n:
No verb 'to be', and none is wanted: 'governing-the-state-by-cleverness | the state's robber'. Two noun phrases set side by side, and the English 'is' is our addition.

賊 is not a sneak-thief but the robber who takes by force. Wang Bi's comment is worth having: move the people by cunning and they learn your devices and dodge them, so you contrive further, and the deceit multiplies on both sides.

賊 and the 福 that answers it in the next unit rhymed in Old Chinese — both belong to the 職 rhyme group. In Mandarin, zéi against fú, there is nothing left of it.

sentences.t:
不以智治國，
國之福。
知此兩者亦稽式。
常知稽式，
是謂玄德。
玄德深矣，
遠矣，

morph.gloss: good fortune, the good that comes down on a man
the two of them, this pair
the one(s) that — makes a noun of what precedes
the standard to measure by — the model that old and new alike are checked against; some recensions write 楷式, 'a pattern to copy'
to check against, to compare — Wang Bi glosses it 同, 'the same, held in common'
a model, a pattern, a norm
to check against; Wang Bi: 同, 'held in common'
this (a demonstrative — Classical Chinese has no verb 'to be')
is called, is spoken of as
dark — the blue-black of water too deep to see into
potency — the power a thing has by simply being what it is
(final particle) — marks the thing as now settled: 'and there it is'

sentences.l:
not to govern the state by cleverness —
the state's good fortune.
To know these two is also the standard to measure by.
Abidingly to know the standard —
this is called dark potency.
Dark potency is deep,
is far,
sentences.i: not to govern a state by cleverness is its good fortune. To know both of these is likewise the standard to measure by; and to know that standard always is what is called dark potency. Dark potency runs deep, and reaches far,
sentences.n:
稽式 is the chapter's term of art, and the recensions do not agree on how to write it — some print 楷式, 'a pattern to copy from'. Wang Bi glosses 稽 as 同, 'the same, held in common', and takes the phrase for the standard that old and new alike are measured against. The English follows him, as the sole-source rule requires.

矣 is not a full stop. It marks a state as newly reached and now settled, so 深矣，遠矣 is less 'it is deep and far' than 'deep it is; far it is' — the point arrived at, twice over.

玄德 is 'dark potency', each word as this book uses it: 玄 the blue-black of unfathomable water, 德 the power a thing has by being what it is. It is two words, not one — you have met both halves apart — but the pair recurs, in chapters 10 and 51 as well as here.

morph.gloss: with, together with (yǔ; the same character is yù 'to take part' and yú, a final particle)
to turn back, to go the reverse way, to come round again

sentences.i: turning back along with all things —
sentences.n: 反 is the Way's own motion all through this book — chapter 40 makes it the Way's very movement: turning back, going the reverse way, coming round again. Wang Bi reads it here as a return: 反其真, 'back to what is genuine in them'. The other reading — that dark potency runs counter to things — sits just as well on the same three characters. The English here follows Wang Bi, as the sole-source rule requires, and the other reading is on the record in this note.

morph.gloss: only after that, and not before — a fixed connective, taken as one word
then, and thereupon — the next link in a chain
to go with the grain of a thing; compliance, falling-in-with

sentences.l: and only then reaches the great going-with.
sentences.i: and only then does it come through to the great accord.
sentences.n:
然後 is a fixed connective, 'only after that'. Its parts are still legible in it — 然 'so' + 後 'after' — which is not true of 是以, where neither half gives you 'therefore'; but the book uses 然後 as a single word, so it is one tap here.

順 is going with the grain: the carpenter's word for cutting the way the wood runs. It answers the 反 of the line before. First the turning back, and only out of that the great falling-in-with.
